newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin active on domestic and foreign fronts.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin active on domestic and foreign fronts.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, in a burst of activity following his return to the Kremlin, promised Russians on Wednesday to tackle two major evils of the state and proposed an international force for a hostage crisis in Peru.

Yeltsin, 65, who returned to work on Monday after almost six months of absence due to heart illness and surgery, said in a radio address that wage and pension delays were the most painful problem for Russia.
He also pledged to deal with abuses by state officials.
"The state's debt to the people is too high and the living standards are intolerably low," Yeltsin, whose voice lacked force but sounded smooth and confident.
Wage delays which amount to trillions of roubles (billions of dollars) have triggered labour protests, including a nationwide strike of coal miners.
Top military officials have warned that morale in the armed forces has sunk to a dangerously low point as most officers have not been paid since the summer.
Yeltsin said stern measures to stop massive tax evasion and impose strong state control over the sale of alchohol could provide funds to help solve the problem of wage delays.
He said widespread misuse of state funds by civil servants also badly affected the budget and added to the crisis.
"It's time to take measures against those who like living luxuriously at the state expense, or to be more exact at the expense of ordinary people," Yeltsin said.
"Officials in charge will have to answer for wrongdoings. If someone is stealing he should go to jail, if someone is incompetent he should resign," he said.
Yeltsin is clearly seeking a high domestic and international profile to highlight his return to the Kremlin.
He launched a surprise proposal later on Wednesday by proposing that Russia and the Group of Seven rich nations join forces to help resolve the hostage crisis in Peru.

He suggested that a joint declaration of the "Group of Eight" -- the G7 plus Russia -- should offer "coordinated assistance in resolving the conflict including possible dispatch there of special anti-terrorist squads from national security services".
If Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori agreed, special services of the eight countries should set up a joint group "with the aim of launching an operation to free the hostages".
In a separate letter to Fujimori, Yeltsin said Russia, which had none of its citizens caught up in the hostage drama, was ready to send its own anti-terrorist group to Lima.
"The situation in Lima requires that we should show in practice how we are able to act in order to help defenceless people who have become victims of terrorists," said Yeltsin's letter to Fujimori.

Russia's special services, especially the Federal Security Service, has suffered a series of public setbacks during Moscow's 21-month abortive attempt to bring Chechen separatists to heel by military methods.

Rebels belonging to the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement seized hundreds of hostages at a Japanese embassy reception in the Peruvian capital last Tuesday. More than 100 of them, including six ambassadors, are still in their hands.
In his radio address, Yeltsin said that the first shot in his new crusade will be made on Thursday at a meeting of a state commission set up to handle tax and non-payment crises.
"I am drafting special measures to correct this intolerable situation," Yeltsin said. "Tomorrow at the meeting of All-Russian Extraordinary Commission serious and strong steps will be taken."
